title: Pneuma: A Large-Scale Real-World Time Series Benchmark for Commercial Aircraft Predictive Maintenance
abstract: Predictive maintenance is vital for commercial aviation, yet progress remains hindered by the lack of public, large-scale real-world datasets. As a result, most methods are developed and evaluated on proprietary data, limiting reproducibility. We introduce Pneuma, the first publicly available large-scale benchmark for predictive maintenance using onboard time series from in-service commercial aircraft. Built around bleed air systems, Pneuma contains over 920 million multivariate time steps across four aircraft types and 9 verified fault scenarios, directly aligned with real maintenance logs. The dataset exhibits key real-world challenges, including substantial class imbalance, subtle fault evolution patterns, and significant variance across aircraft configurations. We structure the benchmark around three tasks: multivariate forecasting, supervised fault classification, and unsupervised anomaly detection, with labels derived from actual maintenance records. Under unified settings, we evaluate over 25 models from four methodological families on 9 carefully curated subsets. The results reveal that even strong contemporary models struggle with subtle fault signatures. Further analyses show consistent gains from additional in-context examples and multivariate inference, while forecasting quality is strongly associated with anomaly detection performance. Together, these findings provide practical insights into effectively modeling complex real-world aviation time series. We hope Pneuma will serve as a rigorous and reproducible foundation for advancing data-driven predictive maintenance toward real-world deployment in commercial aviation.
ai_summary: Pneuma is the first publicly available large-scale benchmark for predictive maintenance using onboard time series from in-service commercial aircraft . It contains over 920 million multivariate time steps across four aircraft types and 9 verified fault scenarios, directly aligned with real maintenance logs .

title: When uncertainty quantification fails: structural vulnerabilities and corrections for selective prediction under clinical class imbalance
abstract: Background. Selective prediction systems improve the safety of clinical artificial intelligence by deferring ambiguous cases to human experts while automating high-confidence decisions. However, this safety mechanism relies entirely on the premise that uncertainty scores accurately reflect clinical ambiguity. In prognostic tasks characterized by severe class imbalance, where the clinical outcome of interest is a minority, this assumption breaks down. Standard uncertainty measures cease to capture clinically aligned ambiguity; instead, they become a proxy for class membership, systematically penalizing minority patients regardless of their individual predictive clarity. Results. Across 56 synthetic conditions and three neurodegenerative cohorts spanning severe class imbalance to near-balanced conditions (multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's Disease, Alzheimer's Disease), our framework consistently maintained bounded, balanced risk across trajectories. In contrast, global metrics either collapsed minority Sensitivity or protected the minority at the expense of majority patients. Applying CCR with standard entropy fails to protect the minority because it breaks within-class monotonicity when tau=0.5. Combining CCR with threshold-aware metrics restores strict monotonicity, correctly identifies ambiguous patients, and safely mitigates minority exclusion. Conclusions. Under clinical class imbalance, standard uncertainty quantification measures dataset sparsity rather than clinical ambiguity, creating a systemic illusion of safety. This bias is a correctable structural flaw. Clinical pipelines deploying selective prediction under imbalance should adopt threshold-aligned uncertainty measures and class-stratified evaluation. This reduces class-specific risk imbalance, supporting safer selective prediction under the evaluated conditions without silently excluding the most vulnerable patients.
ai_summary: Selective prediction systems improve the safety of clinical artificial intelligence by deferring ambiguous cases to human experts . But this safety mechanism relies entirely on the premise that uncertainty scores accurately reflect clinical ambiguity .

title: Collective Dynamics of Self-Reinforcement: How Cross-Task Coupling Drives Policy Collapse in Unsupervised RLVR
abstract: Label-free reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) rewards a language model for agreeing with its own majority vote. It improves reasoning at first but eventually collapses: the self-assessed reward goes to one while accuracy falls, often until the model gives the same answer to every problem. The collapse appears only when training uses many problems. We explain this dataset-size dependence as a collective instability. In a solvable many-problem model in which problems share parameters, a population whose problems prefer different answers amplifies any shared perturbation for as long as the population-averaged slope $\langle F'\rangle$ of the single-problem self-reinforcement drift $F$ is positive. This holds while problems are still uncertain about their answers. Per-problem sharpening, slowed by $1/N$ for $N$ training problems, races against the shared mode, which grows at a rate $\proptoλ^2$ independent of $N$, where $λ$ is the strength of the shared coupling. This yields a critical number of problems $N_c\simeq\ln(1/δ)/(λ^2G)$, where $δ$ seeds the shared mode and $G$ decreases with the initial confidence. Simulations of the model confirm the predictions: a sharp transition, $N_c\proptoλ^{-2}$ up to a logarithmic correction, a single critical amplification $λ^2NG$ across couplings, confidence profiles and training variants, a logarithmic dependence on batch size, and no collapse for confident initial models. A kernel version of the theory identifies a protective coupling (generalization of sharpening) and a marginal-entropy bonus that stabilizes the uniform collective mode. In label-free RL of a small Transformer, removing the shared direction prevents collapse entirely, restoring it causes collapse, and collapse grows with training-set size and base-model entropy.

title: Kinematic Constraint-Referenced Evaluation for Articulated Object Manipulation
abstract: Manipulation policies are evaluated predominantly by binary task success, which cannot tell whether the commanded gesture is the one the object's kinematics admit. We introduce Constraint-Referenced Strategy (CRS), which projects the commanded end-effector twist onto the object's joint axis, separating progress along the joint from off-constraint waste. CRS requires a joint model and a joint-following scripted controller derived from it, but no recorded demonstration or learned judge. On 74 simulated articulated objects, success registers three transfer failures as lower rates but attributes none, while the two CRS channels give each a distinct signature. A door-trained behavior-cloning policy opens drawers in 59 of 110 episodes, and in these passes it commands about $40\times$ the off-axis rotation of a drawer-trained policy's passes ($1.27$ vs.\ $0.032$~rad/s). Relative to a scripted controller scored with the same axis, CRS verdicts are unchanged under joint-axis errors up to $30^\circ$; absolute thresholds tolerate about $8^\circ$.

title: When, Where, and What to Correct: Human-Guided Adaptive Residual Correction for Robot Policies
abstract: Imitation policies that reliably execute most of a manipulation trajectory can still fail in localized regions requiring last-mile precision. Updating the full policy or exploring residual actions everywhere treats this local failure as a global learning problem. We introduce Adaptive Residual Correction (ARC), a lightweight post-training module that uses reinforcement learning (RL) to learn a residual correction on top of a frozen policy while using sparse human corrections to structure autonomous exploration. Rather than treating human corrections as imitation targets, ARC uses pre-intervention states to determine 'when' residual control should become active and correction geometry to determine 'where' in residual action space autonomous refinement should explore; task reward determines 'what' residual is ultimately executed. Across three precision-manipulation tasks on a real robot, ARC improves average task success from 33.3% to 75.0%. The human corrections define task-dependent 2-3 dimensional subspaces of the seven-joint residual space that retain 96.0-97.7% of squared correction magnitude. Together, these results show that sparse human corrections can localize and constrain autonomous post-training without requiring the observed correction itself to serve as the final action target.

title: GroundControl: Satellite-Conditioned Multi-View Diffusion for Reconstruction-Free Novel View Synthesis
abstract: Multi-view or video diffusion models have recently emerged as state-of-the-art approaches for novel-view synthesis from sparse image collections. While they can produce high quality images, they tend to hallucinate unrealistic spatial layouts when synthesizing views outside the input views (scene extrapolation). We propose to address this challenge for outdoor scenes by using satellite images as an additional information source to condition the multi-view generative model. We introduce a new satellite-conditioned multi-view diffusion model that combines conditioning from a satellite image and street-level input images when generating novel-views. Our cross-attention based conditioning allows us to retain pretrained multi-view diffusion priors to generate seamless, realistic, novel views from a handful of source views, while also adhering to the scene layout as seen from satellite images. Our model does not use 3D scene reconstruction, and only relies on posed street and satellite views. Our experiments on outdoor datasets show that our model is better than both satellite-conditioned or street-view conditioned baselines on novel-view synthesis, especially on challenging cases where target views have very little overlap with source views. title: Which Hand Was Late? Diagnosis for Robot Failure Recovery in Bimanual Tool Use
abstract: Failure diagnosers for robot manipulation are increasingly vision--language models (VLMs), trained and evaluated on single-arm failures produced by perturbing a successful demonstration. Bimanual tool use adds failures of other kinds: a tool that slips out of its socket while still held, two correct gestures made at different times, and attempts that fail for two reasons at once. On a simulated bimanual tool-use task whose failure causes are read from the recorded trace, we measure what each sensing channel lets a diagnoser tell. The tool's slip is read on the tool hand; which hand was late is read on both arms, while a sensor on one hand reads its own hand's delay and at most part of the other's; and whether a late attempt was also pushed too weakly is not identifiable from passive sensing when the tool hand is late. Within two attempts, a repair policy that escalates when the cause is not identifiable repairs as many failures as one told the true cause. A VLM's internal state carries the late hand almost perfectly, along a direction no closer to the one its answer reads than a random one; whether the answer reports it depends on the wording of the question.

title: GTFormer: A Syntax-Free Graph Network Alternative to Transformers for 8192$\times$ Length Extrapolation in Linear Time
abstract: Self-attention mechanisms have established the Transformer as the dominant backbone across natural language processing, source code intelligence, and automated theorem proving. However, all-to-all pairwise token comparison enforces a quadratic $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ compute and memory barrier alongside severe softmax attention dilution as sequence length $N$ scales beyond the training horizon. Inspired by recent advances in algebraic graph learning (\textbf{WPNet}), this work introduces \textbf{GTFormer}, a syntax-free hierarchical Graph Neural Network (GNN) that replaces flat self-attention for general long-context sequence modeling. GTFormer organizes raw token streams into a bounded-degree hierarchy combining a balanced binary reduction tree ($\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ depth), horizontal boundary-bridging shift edges, random expander shortcuts, multi-channel convex highway gating, and a top-down broadcast pass. Across eight long-context code, log, and multi-hop retrieval benchmarks trained exclusively on sequences of length $N \le 512$, GTFormer extrapolates zero-shot to $N = 4{,}194{,}304$ ($8192\times$) on a single commodity GPU in linear $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, maintaining near-perfect accuracy where standard and RoPE Transformers suffer from out-of-distribution attention collapse and out-of-memory exhaustion.

title: The Structure Gap: When More Data Cannot Replace Structured Reasoning
abstract: A persistent belief in modern AI is that sufficiently large learners trained on sufficiently much data can make explicit domain knowledge optional. This paper examines a limitation of that belief. We define structure-encoded problems: tasks whose input-output map is determined, or sharply constrained, by known structure such as a solver, symmetry group, graph, physical law, measurement operator, grammar, combinatorial search space, or optimization objective. For such tasks, the central question is not expressivity--a dense neural network may contain the desired map--but finite-data identification, extrapolation, and certification. We introduce the structure gap: the finite-resource gap between a method that receives the governing structure and a learner that receives only examples. The strongest useful form of the claim is asymptotic rather than absolute: structure-agnostic learning may approach a structured solver as coverage grows, but every finite dataset can leave residual uncertainty that the structure resolves by construction. We prove this exactly for a Gaussian inverse problem: the known-operator Wiener solver attains Bayes risk, while the dense empirical learner in the correct linear class has persistent expected excess risk. We also prove a cell-coverage lower bound and an unobserved-orbit non-identifiability result. Controlled experiments in known-operator inversion, sparse recovery, and graph reachability with size extrapolation instantiate the mechanisms. When validated structure is available, it can constrain the hypothesis space before learning begins, leaving learning to address components the structure does not specify.
ai_summary: The strongest useful form of the claim is asymptotic rather than absolute: structure-agnostic learning may approach a structured solver as coverage grows .

title: Orthogonal and Parametrized Multi-Attribute Steering of LLMs
abstract: Activation steering offers an effective and efficient way to modify an LLM's behavior at inference time. However, it remains unclear how to apply steering such that the signal is consistently strong and the steering strength has a universally interpretable meaning. We address this first by identifying the most steerable interval for each steering vector and rescaling the steering range accordingly. Building on this, we introduce a more interpretable method for steering, called parameterized steering which instead of pushing activations in a direction, it sets them at the desired trait strength. Next, with multi-trait steering, we find that naively combining vectors causes them to interfere with one another. In response, we develop a method to orthogonalize the vectors; it decouples these traits, allowing a model to exhibit one behavior without inducing the others, thus enabling multiple traits to be steered simultaneously.

title: A note on data-efficient finetuning of vision foundation models
abstract: Adapting foundation models to a new task within or beyond the training domain is the de facto standard for building specialized machine learning models. Recently, Visual Prompting (VP) has emerged as a promising technique for efficient knowledge transfer. As new foundation model families~(like Mamba) get introduced and VP pipelines such as AutoVP reach greater maturity, we find a growing need for a systematic evaluation of current approaches. In this work, we assess the performance of the latest models, comparing them to earlier architectures and alternative fine-tuning methods, to better understand the progress, challenges and opportunities in the field of efficient fine-tuning under resource limitations. Towards this goal, this paper provides a concise empirical overview of the interactions among foundation model families (Attention-, Convolution-, and Mamba-based) and transfer paradigms: VP, Linear Probing (LP), Full Fine-tuning (FFT) and Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA). Our work builds up on previous findings by broadening the selection of evaluated models and techniques while tuning hyperparameters. In the interest of delivering practical guidelines for the user, we also explore application of prevalent regularization techniques to boost performance in the context of VP.

title: Strategyproof Deep Reinforcement Learning for Online Resource Allocation
abstract: Online resource allocation faces two coupled challenges: (1) allocating scarce resources efficiently under uncertain future demand, and (2) ensuring that agents report task valuations and requirements truthfully (strategyproofness). Reinforcement Learning (RL) adapts allocation decisions through experience but does not necessarily ensure strategyproofness. Existing strategyproof RL uses a linear allocation rule, which limits the resource interactions it can represent. Neural mechanism design methods offer greater expressiveness, but provide only approximate incentive guarantees. Against this background, we introduce the first strategyproof deep RL mechanism for online resource allocation. It integrates three novel components: (i) a monotonic neural network that learns nonlinear interactions by construction (higher reported value cannot reduce acceptance, while a longer reported duration or larger resource requirement cannot increase it); (ii) a generalised critical payment: the lowest accepted value, with all other inputs fixed; and (iii) training by either RL or imitation of an existing rule. Together, monotonicity and the critical payment ensure strategyproofness and individual rationality, while the neural rule provides flexibility and imitation improves training efficiency. Empirically, on a four-resource stream with two partner pairs that a linear difference cannot represent, the neural rule achieves 97.8% of an offline welfare upper bound, compared with 93.8% for a linear learner and 89.0% for first-come, first-served, closing 65% and 80% of the remaining optimality gap, respectively. Moreover, imitation reaches 97.5% in only 261 seconds, about 89 times faster than RL.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) adapts allocation decisions through experience but does not necessarily ensure strategyproofness . Existing strategyproof RL uses a linear allocation rule, which limits the resource interactions it can represent .

title: Long-term quality of life, rehospitalization risks, and economic viability of remote cardiac rehabilitation: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Although remote cardiac rehabilitation (RCR) is a promising alternative to traditional center-based care, evidence regarding its exact impact on health-related quality of life (HRQoL), cardiovascular safety, and economic viability remains fragmented, necessitating a comprehensive synthesis to guide clinical implementation. This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to evaluate the HRQoL, cardiovascular safety, and economic viability of RCR versus standard center-based care in cardiovascular disease, with subgroup analyses based on follow-up duration and high-risk patient cohorts. Literature searches were conducted across multiple databases, including PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, supplemented by manual screening of relevant references to identify clinical studies on RCR up to July 2026. Two independent review teams performed data extraction and risk of bias assessment using the RevMan software. Meta-analyses were conducted employing random-effects models to calculate pooled effect sizes with corresponding 95% confidence intervals. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Cochrane Q test and  A total of 45 randomized controlled trials were included in this meta-analysis. RCR significantly improved HRQoL across multiple scales (MacNew: MD = 0.17; MLHFQ: MD = -5.38;  RCR may serve as an effective and safe alternative to conventional care that improves physical and psychological well-being, was associated with a lower risk of cardiac rehospitalization, and may provide economic value in certain healthcare systems. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261374977, PROSPERO CRD420261374977.

title: Integrating knowledge graphs and retrieval-augmented generation to identify clinical pharmacology gaps in infectious disease trial protocols.
abstract: Clinical trial protocols contain critical clinical pharmacology information that is often scattered across different sections of these lengthy documents. The purpose was to evaluate whether a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) protocol review integrated with knowledge graphs (KGs) could be used to obtain clinical pharmacology evidence and identify regulatory gaps. Clinical trial protocols were obtained from the Gates Foundation's publicly available corpus of clinical trials in low- and middle-income countries. The RAG protocol review was used to assess the protocols against Food & Drug Administration (FDA) guidance documents for hepatic impairment, exposure-response, population PK (PopPK), and physiologically based pharmacokinetic modeling (PBPK). Disease-specific KG analyses were conducted for tuberculosis (TB), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), malaria, and neglected tropical diseases (NTD). KG models connecting studies to drugs, diseases, pharmacologic classes, organ-function exclusions, biomarkers, and pharmacokinetic (PK) parameter features were obtained. Across 42 unique trials, the KG contained 223 nodes and 376 edges. TB protocols produced the largest disease-specific graph, whereas HIV had the highest frequency of PK studies. Gap analysis showed that hepatic impairment exclusions in TB were more frequent than PK studies. In the multi-guidance evaluation, faithfulness was high, answer relevancy was lower, and the clinical pharmacology metric showed guidance-dependent differences. The integrated KG-RAG approach can help highlight potential gaps in clinical pharmacology reporting in infectious disease clinical trial protocols.

title: Hypothesis-generating network toxicology analysis of potential molecular convergence between a polystyrene oligomer proxy and papillary thyroid carcinoma.
abstract: Polystyrene microplastics (PS-MPs) are emerging environmental contaminants with endocrine-disrupting and pro-inflammatory effects, but whether PS-MPs-associated molecular targets converge with papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) alterations remains unclear. This hypothesis-generating study aimed to identify candidate molecular networks and cellular contexts shared between a simplified polystyrene computational proxy and PTC. Putative targets from CTD and from TargetNet/SwissTargetPrediction using a five-styrene-unit oligomer proxy were intersected with thyroid cancer-related genes from OMIM and GeneCards. Protein functional-association and enrichment analyses were followed by differential expression analysis in GSE33630 (45 normal and 49 PTC samples). LASSO and SVM-RFE identified core genes; stability was examined by repeated nested resampling conditional on the seven-gene candidate panel. Individual-gene tumor-normal discrimination was assessed in GSE33630 and GSE60542. Protein patterns were evaluated qualitatively in the Human Protein Atlas and preliminarily in 15 matched PTC-adjacent tissue pairs. CIBERSORT-estimated immune fractions and two single-cell datasets were analyzed as exploratory context. Among 144 putative proxy-associated targets and 2,139 thyroid cancer-related genes, 75 were shared. Seven candidates overlapped with 1,306 PTC differentially expressed genes, and BCL2, BAX, and FN1 were selected by both feature-selection methods and remained stable across the tested GeneCards thresholds and CTD-only sensitivity analysis. BCL2 was downregulated, whereas BAX and FN1 were upregulated in PTC; individual-gene AUCs were 0.963, 0.941, and 0.965 in GSE33630 and 0.942, 0.907, and 0.955 in GSE60542. HPA images and clinical IHC supported the same protein-level directions. After multiple-testing correction, only the CIBERSORT-estimated neutrophil fraction differed between groups (higher in PTC; q=0.0021). Single-cell analysis localized the three genes across epithelial, stromal, and immune compartments. BCL2, BAX, and FN1 are candidate molecular nodes at the convergence of polystyrene-proxy annotations and PTC-associated alterations. The findings do not demonstrate patient PS-MPs exposure, intact-particle effects, or causality, and require validation in material-characterized exposure experiments and exposure-aware clinical studies.

title: Explainable residual CNN with Gramian Angular Field encoding for rapid quantification of soil properties using near-infrared spectroscopy.
abstract: Soil chemical composition is a key indicator of soil fertility, yet conventional physicochemical analysis is time-consuming and costly. Although near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy enables rapid, non-destructive detection, traditional linear models struggle with the non-linear nature of high-dimensional spectral data, and deep-learning models often suffer from a "black-box" problem. A one-dimensional residual convolutional neural network (1D-Res-CNN) was constructed, and the output feature maps of intermediate convolutional layers were visualized to reveal how the model learns spectral features. One-dimensional spectral sequences were mapped into twodimensional images via Gramian Angular Summation Field (GASF) and Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT); after systematically comparing encoding performance across spectral sub-intervals, the optimal range was selected to feed a two-dimensional residual CNN (2D-Res-CNN) regression model. Using SNV-preprocessed Fourier-transform NIR spectra and an SPXY-partitioned dataset, the proposed framework was benchmarked against partial least squares regression (PLSR), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), and random forest (RF). First-layer kernels in the 1D-Res-CNN automatically captured spectral features corresponding to functional-group absorption peaks, supporting the physical interpretability of feature extraction. Cognitive transparency and trust calibration in explainable AI systems: a psychological model of human-AI decision reliance.
abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is widely expected to improve transparency and support appropriate human reliance on AI-assisted decision-making. However, the psychological processes through which explainability relates to reliance remain insufficiently understood, and explainability, transparency, and trust have largely been examined separately. This study develops and tests a psychological model of cognitive transparency in which AI explainability, algorithmic transparency, and perceived AI accuracy are associated with human reliance on AI through cognitive understanding, cognitive trust, and trust calibration, with AI literacy as a boundary condition. A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 342 AI users in South Korea in May and June 2026. Each participant evaluated one self-selected AI system that they had personally used; all constructs were measured by self-report. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. AI explainability (β = 0.349) and algorithmic transparency (β = 0.297) were positively associated with cognitive understanding. Cognitive understanding (β = 0.388) and, more strongly, perceived AI accuracy (β = 0.492) were associated with cognitive trust. Cognitive trust was associated with trust calibration (β = 0.631), which was associated with human reliance on AI (β = 0.600). All hypothesized indirect effects were significant, and AI literacy strengthened the association between AI explainability and cognitive understanding (β = 0.192). The model explained 36%-54% of the variance in the endogenous constructs and showed medium predictive power. The findings are consistent with a sequence in which explainable AI relates to reliance through users' understanding and trust judgments. Because all constructs were self-reported and measured at a single point in time, the results describe associations among users' perceptions rather than causal effects, independently verified calibration, or objectively appropriate reliance. The findings suggest that AI developers in domains such as healthcare, education, and finance, where calibrated reliance is critical, should pair user-facing explanations with information about system accuracy and with AI literacy support.

This study develops and tests a psychological model of cognitive transparency .

abstract: Sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) is a major killer of adults in the United States and has a significant recurrence rate. title: Artificial intelligence attitudes, presenteeism, and work engagement among nurses: a structural equation modeling approach.
abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare has transformed clinical practice, yet the psychological mechanisms linking nurses' AI attitudes to their occupational functioning remain insufficiently understood, particularly regarding the role of presenteeism as a potential explanatory pathway. This study aimed to examine the relationships among nurses' attitudes toward AI, presenteeism, and work engagement, and to test the mediating role of presenteeism within a Job Demands-Resources framework. A cross-sectional correlational design was employed, with data collected from 806 hospital nurses across Saudi Arabia and Egypt using the AI Attitude Scale for Nurses, the Presenteeism Scale in Nursing, and the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale. Data were analyzed via structural equation modeling with bootstrapped mediation testing (2,000 resamples) and multi-group invariance analysis. Following the exclusion of four multivariate outliers, the final analytic sample comprised 802 nurses. The hypothesized model demonstrated good fit (CFI = 0.981, RMSEA = 0.068). title: Economic policy uncertainty and medical inflation in China: multi-scale linkages and time-varying responses.
abstract: Medical inflation is a central health-system cost pressure, yet little is known about whether economic policy uncertainty (EPU) affects medical prices differently across timescales and historical periods. This paper examines the multi-scale and time-varying relationship between EPU and medical inflation in China using quarterly data from 2004Q1 to 2026Q1, wavelet filtering, and an SV-TVP-FAVAR model. Posterior uncertainty is summarized by the posterior mean and the 16th and 84th percentiles. Positive responses are present in both frequency-specific baseline models. The full-sample posterior-mean maxima for the higher- and lower-frequency EPU components are 0.297 and 0.108; they are 0.214 and 0.208 when the sample ends in 2025Q4. In the three-factor model, aggregate health-care CPI reaches 0.237 for a shock dated 2020Q2 at an eight-quarter horizon (central 68% credible interval [0.063, 0.412]). The eight-quarter posterior band overlaps those at several earlier dates, and the estimated magnitude varies with factor count. In the baseline full-sample specification, western medicine prices have the largest consumer-side posterior-mean maximum, reaching 0.424 for a shock dated 2020Q3 at six quarters (central 68% credible interval [0.231, 0.618]), although the exact peak date varies across specifications. Traditional Chinese medicine prices and medical service CPI show smaller positive responses, while pharmaceutical manufacturing PPI provides complementary evidence from the production side. Overall, the results show that the EPU-medical inflation relationship varies across EPU frequency scales, historical dates, and health-price components.
